content: Hemocyanins, also spelled haemocyanins, are respiratory proteins classified as metalloproteins. They contain two copper atoms that reversibly bind a single oxygen molecule (O₂). Upon oxygenation, hemocyanins undergo a color change from a colorless Cu(I) deoxygenated form to a blue Cu(II) oxygenated form. These proteins are responsible for oxygen transport in the blood of most mollusks and some arthropods, such as the horseshoe crab. Hemocyanins are second only to hemoglobin in their prevalence as oxygen transport molecules in biological systems. Although hemocyanins perform a respiratory function similar to hemoglobin, their molecular structure and mechanism differ significantly. Hemoglobin carries its iron atoms within porphyrin rings (heme groups), whereas the copper atoms in hemocyanins are coordinated as prosthetic groups by histidine residues. Hemocyanins are commonly found in crustaceans that inhabit cold environments with low oxygen pressure, where hemoglobin is less efficient at oxygen transport. Under these conditions, hemocyanins demonstrate superior oxygen transport efficiency. Most hemocyanins bind oxygen non-cooperatively and are approximately one-fourth as efficient as hemoglobin in transporting oxygen per unit of blood. Hemoglobin exhibits cooperative oxygen binding due to steric conformational changes in its protein complex, which increase its oxygen affinity as it becomes partially oxygenated. The Hill constants for hemoglobin vary depending on the species and experimental conditions. In cases where hemocyanins exhibit cooperative binding, they are organized into protein sub-complexes of six subunits (hexamers), each with one oxygen-binding site. Binding of oxygen to one unit in the hexamer increases the oxygen affinity of neighboring units. These hexamer complexes are further arranged into larger complexes composed of dozens of hexamers. One study demonstrated that cooperative binding in hemocyanins depends on the arrangement of hexamers within the larger complex, suggesting inter-hexamer cooperative binding. The oxygen-binding profile of hemocyanins is also influenced by dissolved salt ion concentrations and pH. Hemocyanins are composed of multiple individual subunit proteins, each containing two copper atoms capable of binding one oxygen molecule (O₂). Each subunit has a molecular weight of approximately 75 kilodaltons (kDa). Depending on the species, these subunits may be arranged into dimers or hexamers, which are further organized into chains or clusters with molecular weights exceeding 1500 kDa. The subunits are typically homogeneous or heterogeneous, with two variant subunit types. Due to their large size, hemocyanins are usually found free-floating in the blood, unlike hemoglobin, which is contained within cells to prevent clogging and damage to blood-filtering organs such as the kidneys. This free-floating nature allows hemocyanins to achieve higher densities than hemoglobin, thereby increasing oxygen-carrying capacity. However, free-floating hemocyanins can also increase blood viscosity and the energy expenditure required for blood circulation. Spectroscopic analysis of oxygenated hemocyanin (oxyhemocyanin) reveals several notable features. Resonance Raman spectroscopy indicates symmetric oxygen binding, while UV-Vis spectroscopy shows strong absorbances at 350 nm and 580 nm. Oxyhemocyanin is electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR)-silent, indicating the absence of unpaired electrons. Infrared spectroscopy reveals an O-O stretching frequency (ν(O-O)) of 755 cm⁻¹, which rules out a mononuclear peroxo complex and does not align with the UV-Vis spectra of mononuclear peroxo or Kenneth Karlin's trans-peroxo models. The O-O bond in oxyhemocyanin is considerably weaker compared to Karlin's trans-peroxo model. In contrast, Nobumasa Kitajima's model, which shows an O-O stretching frequency of 741 cm⁻¹ and UV-Vis absorbances at 349 nm and 551 nm, aligns well with experimental observations for oxyhemocyanin. The weak O-O bond in oxyhemocyanin is attributed to metal-ligand backdonation into the σ-orbitals. This involves the donation of electrons into the O-O antibonding orbitals, which weakens the O-O bond and results in a lower-than-expected infrared stretching frequency.
